en: Oṃ, salutation to the embodiment of auspiciousness!
Now begins the *Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*.
Salutation to Śiva, who eternally performs the fivefold cosmic acts.

For the sake of pacifying the poison of saṃsāra, the essence is being extracted safely from the great ocean of the *Pratyabhijñā*, which is the quintessence of the Upaniṣads of Śaṅkara, for the purpose of illuminating the supreme reality of one's own self as a mass of consciousness and bliss.

Here, for those few devoted ones of delicate intellect— who have not undergone the arduous labor of studying the treatises on sharp logic, yet who desire the supreme immersion (samāveśa) awakened by the descent of power (śaktipāta)— the reality of the instruction on the Recognition of the Lord (Īśvarapratyabhijñā) is briefly unveiled. In that regard:

In order to manifest that one's own self-deity alone is the cause everywhere, is attainable through easy means, and yields great fruit, he says: "Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the manifestation of the universe. (1)

The cause for the accomplishment, manifestation, maintenance— which consists in resting within the supreme subject— and withdrawal of the entire universe, from Sadāśiva down to the earth, is the Blessed Lady herself, the independent consciousness in the form of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), consisting of the unsurpassed reflective awareness (anuttara-vimarśa), non-different from the venerable Lord Śiva.

This is the reason: for when this [power] expands, the world opens its eyes and remains established; and when its expansion ceases, it closes its eyes. One's own direct experience alone is the witness here.
As for anything else—such as *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and so forth—which is distinct from the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), it does not manifest at all.

Because it is non-existent, it possesses no causality whatsoever; however, insofar as it is manifest, consciousness—whose nature is light—is itself the cause, since it is identical with that manifestation, and not some other thing.
For this very reason, space, time, and form are created by this [consciousness] and sustained by its vital breath; they do not constitute its true essence.

The phrase "sufficient to break" implies that this [consciousness] possesses a nature that is pervasive, eternally manifest, and complete; this is indeed what is established by the sense of the passage.
Now, one might object: "Is the world not entirely non-different from consciousness? And if there is no difference, how can there be the relationship of cause and effect? To this it is replied:
The Blessed Consciousness alone, whose nature is pure and autonomous,
manifests as the self of each and every infinite world; this is the ultimate reality of the relationship between cause and effect.
And since this very [consciousness] is the cause for the establishment and manifestation of the universe— which consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— therefore,
for the establishment of this [consciousness], which is autonomous, undivided, and self-luminous by nature, there is the manifestation of ever-new objects.
Neither is the wretched means of valid cognition employed, nor is it logically established.
As it is said in the *Trikasāra*:
"Just as one strives to leap over the shadow of one's own head by means of one's own feet..."
"The head should not be at the level of the feet; so too is this *baindavī* digit.

Since she is the cause for the accomplishment of the universe and for its withdrawal—which consists in bringing it into the state of equilibrium with the supreme non-duality—she is therefore autonomous (*svatantrā*).
Having recognized its own sovereignty,
she is the cause of all worldly accomplishments, which consist of both enjoyment and liberation;
thus it should be explained by way of repetition.

Moreover, the "means" (*upāya*) for its thorough knowledge is that very attainment (*siddhi*) of the universe— consisting of the blue, pleasure, body, vital breath, and so forth— which, through the process of ascending the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is the immersion into the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
And by this, the state of being an easy means has been stated; as it was said in the *Śrīvijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
"The cognition of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings."
"But for yogins, this is the distinction: attentiveness toward the connection.
Thus, the singular number in the word "citi" (consciousness), by expressing its being unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, reveals the unreality of all doctrines asserting duality.
The word *svatantra* (independent), expressing its distinction from the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*), declares that consciousness has sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) as its essence.
The phrase beginning with "the universe" (*viśva*) indicates its possession of all powers, its being the cause of everything, and its being an easy means [to liberation].
And he said that it has great fruit.
Now, one might object: "If consciousness is the cause of the universe, then, given its dependence on material causes and so forth, the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda) would not be abandoned.
Anticipating this, he says:
By its own will, it unfolds the universe upon its own wall. // 2 //
It is by its own will, and not by the will of another like Brahmā and so forth;
and it is by that very [will], and not in dependence upon material causes and the like.
For if it were otherwise, the aforementioned sovereignty would be lost, and consciousness itself could not be established.
On its own wall, and not anywhere else,
the universe previously determined appears like a city in a mirror— undivided [from it].
It causes that which is as if divided to unfold;
and unfolding is the manifestation of that which already exists.
By this, it is stated that the world exists in a state of identity with light alone.
Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of the universe through its divisions, he says:
"That [universe] is manifold, due to the distinction between the corresponding objects of cognition and the subjects of cognition. (3)
That universe is manifold, meaning it exists in many different ways;
how so? Because of the distinction and variety between the objects of cognition and the subjects of cognition, which are mutually appropriate and exist in a state of mutual suitability.

And likewise, within the principle of Sadāśiva, just as the universe— which consists of an indistinct "this-ness" (idantā) veiled by "I-ness" (ahantā)— is the object of perception in its intermediate (parāpara) form, so too is the class of subjects known as the Mantramaheśvaras, presided over by the venerable Lord Sadāśiva.
The universe, which exists in such a state as fashioned by the will of the Supreme Lord,
consists of the identity-in-common (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*) within the principle of Īśvara; and just as that universe is the object of perception,
so too is the group of Mantreśvaras presided over by the venerable Lord Īśvara of that very same nature.

In the stage of Vidyā (vidyāpada), the mantras—which are presided over by the venerable Lord Ananta (Śrīmadanantabhaṭṭāraka) and divided into many branches and sub-divisions—are the subjects (pramātāraḥ) exactly as they are; likewise, the entire universe (viśvam), which is the object of knowledge (prameyam), has precisely that same nature, with differentiation (bheda) as its sole essence. Above Māyā, such are the Vijñānākalas.

For those whose nature is pure consciousness devoid of agency, their object of knowledge (*prameya*) is precisely that [consciousness] which consists essentially in non-difference from Him and is familiar to them through their prior state as *sakala* and *pralayākala*. For the *pralayakevalins*, who are subjects of the void within *māyā*, the object of knowledge is that which is appropriate to them— namely, that which is as if dissolved.
However, for all those situated within the limits of the earth— whether they be entirely distinct, limited, or otherwise— the object of knowledge is exactly of that same nature;
[this is] with respect to the venerable Lord Śiva who has transcended them.
All entities indeed possess the nature of light alone;
as for the venerable Supreme Śiva,
however, he is a single mass of light consisting of supreme bliss, which is both transcendent of the universe and immanent as the soul of the universe.
In this very manner, everything from Śiva down to the earth vibrates as nothing but non-dual;
yet in reality, there is no other object of perception or perceiver whatsoever.
Rather, it is the venerable Lord Paramaśiva alone who thus vibrates through thousands of diverse manifestations.
This has been explained almost entirely.
And just as the Blessed One has the universe as his body, so too the conscious self, whose nature is the contraction of consciousness, consists of the contracted universe.

The illustrious Supreme Śiva, desiring to manifest the universe— which exists in identity with His own self— in the appropriate forms beginning with Sadāśiva, first [manifests it] as the nature of the "void beyond the void" (śūnyātiśūnya), a synonym for the Unconditioned Śiva (anāśrita-śiva), which consists of the non-manifestation of the unity of consciousness, through non-difference from Light.
It flashes forth as manifest luminosity;

from that, it also expands as the nature of all principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and entities (*bhāva*), as well as their respective subjects (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, in the form of the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*). Just as the Lord (*Bhagavān*) thus has the universe as his body, so too does [the limited subject] consist of the contraction of consciousness.
The conscious perceiver, whose nature is consciousness, is contracted; like the seed-pod of a banyan tree, he possesses the entire form of the universe in a contracted state.
And thus says the statement of the established doctrine:
"The form, as well as the one who possesses form, is the destroyer of all forms. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Triśiromata*:
"O beloved, now hear about that body which consists of all the gods."
Earth is characterized by solidity, while water is proclaimed to be characterized by fluidity.
Beginning with these words and ending with the passage,
"Triśirobhairava himself, having pervaded the universe, remains established therein," the text declares that the subject (grāhaka) consists precisely of the contracted universe.

And this is the intention here: even this subject, by virtue of his identity with pure luminosity and according to the aforementioned scripture and reasoning, is of one form with Śiva whose body is the universe; it is only because his true nature is unmanifested by the power of Māyā that he appears as if contracted.
Even contraction, when investigated, consists of consciousness alone, because it manifests as identical with consciousness;
otherwise, nothing at all would exist. Thus, everything...
The grasper, whose body is the universe, is none other than the venerable Lord Śiva.
As it has been said by me:
"If non-manifestation does not manifest, then manifestation alone remains."
"If it is manifestation, then because its nature is that of manifestation, only manifestation remains.
With this very intention, it is stated in the venerable *Spandaśāstra*:
"Since the individual soul consists of everything... [and so forth].
Having begun thus, it is stated by him [in the *Śivasūtravimarśinī*]:
"In the investigations into word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva," and so forth;
by such passages, the non-difference between Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed declared.
The thorough knowledge of this very reality is liberation, and the lack of thorough knowledge of this very reality is bondage; this will surely come to pass.

Now, one might object: "This subject consists of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptualization is caused by the mind (*citta*). Since the mind exists, how can this [subject] have the nature of *śiva*? Anticipating this doubt, he speaks in order to lead us toward the very nature of the mind:
"Consciousness (*cit*) itself, having descended from the state of pure sentience (*cetana*), is that which undergoes contraction through the objects of thought (*cetya*)."
The mind. // 5 //
That which is called "mind" (citta) is nothing other than that very Blessed Lady herself.
For when she conceals her own essential nature (svarūpa) and assumes contraction, then there are two possible courses: sometimes...
Even when expansion has been eclipsed by contraction, it manifests through the predominance of consciousness; sometimes it does so through the predominance of contraction.
In the case where consciousness is predominant, it manifests as primarily consisting of innate luminosity alone.

The state of being devoid of consciousness (*vijñānākala*) [occurs when the subject] is primarily characterized by the reflective awareness of light; however, when that same subjectivity is dominated by the reflective awareness of light, it constitutes the state of the knower (*vidyā-pramātṛ*). Even there, through the gradual attenuation of contraction, one attains the nature of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita.

When the state of consciousness being predominant is acquired through the effort of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the subjectivity of the pure path (*śuddhādhva*) becomes increasingly perfected step by step;
however, when contraction is predominant, there arises the subjectivity of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth. Thus it is.
When [the state] is established, consciousness itself— having assumed the form of a contracted subject, descended from the level of pure sentience (*cetanā*),
and being intent upon grasping objects— becomes contracted by the object of cognition, such as blue or pleasure;
it is indeed contracted by the contraction of both.
And likewise:

"The knowledge and the activity of the Lord regarding the entities that are the forms of his own limbs are Māyā; these same two, along with the third, are the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*)," and so forth. [5]

In the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*, it is stated that the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), manifests in the state of the bound soul (*paśu*) as the powers of knowledge, action, and *māyā*; due to the intensification of contraction, it appears in the form of the mind (*citta*) whose essence consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrītattvagarbhastotra* with the intention of following that [true nature], since the reality of the essential nature exists even during the state of conceptual construction:
"Therefore, those who in any way whatsoever follow the ultimate reality..."
In that state, their own nature as self-luminous does not cease to exist. Thus it is said.
But consciousness alone is the essential nature of the subject of illusion; thus he says: "The subject of illusion consists of that. (6)
The state of body and life-breath is primarily nothing other than mind;
even the ground of emptiness is indeed possessed of mental formations.

Otherwise, for one who has emerged from that state, there would be an absence of pursuing their own duties; therefore, the illusory subject (*pramātā*) consists of nothing but consciousness (*cittamaya*).
With this very intention, in accordance with the actual nature of reality, the *Śivasūtras* state: "The Self is consciousness" (Sūtra 1.1).
Having said this, on the occasion of defining the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), it was further stated: "The mind is the self" (7).
Since liberation results from the correct knowledge of its very true nature, whereas transmigratory existence results from incorrect knowledge,
he speaks in order to analyze this true nature down to its finest details:
"And it is one, twofold, threefold, and fourfold in essence."
Its intrinsic nature consists of seven pentads. // 7 //

From the perspective of definitive discernment, the Self of Consciousness is the one and only Lord Śiva, and not anything else; for it is impossible for light to be divided by space, time, and so forth,
and because it is impossible for that which is insentient to possess the status of a subject.

Since it is precisely Light that, through its own sovereignty, assumes the contraction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and thereby attains the state of being a perceiver of contracted objects, it is thus twofold in nature by virtue of both being of the nature of Light and possessing the manifestation of contraction.
It consists of three aspects because it is veiled by the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*.
It has four natures because its essence consists of the void (*śūnya*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the physical body.
There are seven pentads.
Its essential nature consists of the thirty-five principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth;
likewise, it has the form of the seven types of subjects (pramātṛ) beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala.
Although it possesses the nature of the powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, [it appears otherwise] due to the power of non-recognition (akhyāti).
Because it is enveloped by the sheaths (*kañcuka*) of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*, it possesses the nature of the fivefold group (*pañcaka*).

Thus, when this [Self] is recognized as being of the nature of Śiva alone, as consisting of the thirty-five principles (*tattva*), as having the seven types of subjects (*pramātṛ*) as its essence, and as being composed of the five powers beginning with *acid-śakti*, that is liberation; otherwise, [it is not].
But that is the cause of saṃsāra.
And thus, all philosophical systems belonging to those levels are established in this way. // 8 //

The established positions and doctrines of all schools of thought, such as the Cārvākas and others, are merely artificial roles assumed at will by this Self, like those of an actor. Thus, for instance,
the Cārvākas maintain that the body qualified by consciousness is the Self.

The Naiyāyikas and others consider the self in the cycle of transmigration to consist primarily of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), which serves as the substratum for the multitude of qualities such as cognition; however, upon liberation, when that [intellect] is annihilated, they regard it as being essentially void.

Even the Mīmāṃsakas, who conceive of the self as that which is to be known through the notion of "I" yet whose nature is obscured by limiting adjuncts such as pleasure and pain, are likewise settled upon the intellect alone.
The followers of the Sugata maintain that the continuum of cognition itself is the ultimate reality.
Some knowers of the Upanishads maintain that the self is nothing other than the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). Others,
proponents of the Brahman of non-existence, having plunged into the realm of the void, hold that "this was indeed non-existent" (*asad eva idam āsīt*).

The Mādhyamikas are also exactly like this. The Pāñcarātrikas hold that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (*parā prakṛti*), and that individual souls (*jīvas*) are merely like sparks from him; for they accept the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the supreme primordial nature, which is unmanifest (*avyakta*).
They are thus deeply attached [to their views].
However, the Sāṃkhyas and others rely on a stage that consists for the most part of the discernment of consciousness (*vijñāna-kalā*).
Others, who are knowers of the Upaniṣads, resort to the state of the principle of Īśvara, asserting: "This alone was existent in the beginning."
The grammarians, who occupy the station of the venerable Sadāśiva, maintain that the reality of the Self is the form of Paśyantī, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
In this way, other [points] as well are to be inferred. And thus it is said in the scriptures:
"The Buddhists are established in the reality of consciousness; the Arhats are established in the qualities alone."
Those who know the Vedas abide in the Puruṣa, while the Pāñcarātrikas abide in the Unmanifest.
This has been established by such statements as these:
the Tantrikas [assert] that the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is transcendent of the universe,
while others [assert] that it consists of the universe.
Those established in the traditions of the Kula and other schools,
as well as those who know the systems of Trika and so forth, [recognize Him] as both transcendent to the universe and consisting of the universe.
Thus, all these stages belong to the one Lord alone, whose nature is consciousness, manifested through His sovereignty;
they are differentiated by the varying degrees of the concealment and unveiling of that sovereignty. Therefore, He is indeed one.
The Self has such an extent of pervasion;
however, those of limited vision have been made to grasp a conceit regarding its parts and sub-parts by His very will, whereby [they identify it] with the levels of the body and so forth.
Even when there is the manifestation of the essence of the pervasion of each preceding subject,

those such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others who are colored by attachment to their respective doctrines do not attain the aforementioned Great Pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) without the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*).
“They do not know the supreme God, the omniscient one endowed with wisdom.
“Indeed, Māyā causes them to wander, for they desire liberation where there is no liberation.
And: “Those who worship the Self do not go to the supreme state of Śiva.”
Moreover, those states of all perceptions— the collective cognitions of blue, pleasure, and so forth—
which are inward-turned and constitute rest, belong to that level; they are the means for the manifestation of one's own essential nature, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss.
For instance, whenever an outward-turned form comes to rest within its own essential nature,
at that very moment there occurs the withdrawal of external objects, the abiding in the state of internal tranquility,
and the threading together of the succession of various consciousnesses about to arise; thus, it consists of the union of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
This venerable Goddess of Consciousness, the Fourth (Turīyā), constantly emitting and withdrawing the various distinctions of emanation and so forth,
remains vibrating in a state that is indeed without succession— both full and emaciated, both dual in form and of the nature of neither.
And it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāṭīkā*:
"By the savoring of the object, [the consciousness] arises and becomes full.
And this venerable Goddess, being cultivated more and more progressively, makes [everything] one with her own self.
In this very way, [he protects] the devotee.

If such is the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of the Self, then how is it that this [Self] is described as being "enveloped by impurity," "atomic," "bound by *kalā* and the rest," and "transmigratory"? To this he says:
"Like consciousness (*cidvat*), it is enveloped by impurity due to the contraction of its power; thus it is transmigratory. (9)

When the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, by his own sovereignty immerses himself in the pervasion of non-duality and takes recourse in the pervasion of duality, then His powers— will and the rest— though unrestricted, appear as if they were contracted.
At that very moment, this transmigrating being becomes shrouded in impurity (*mala*).
Thus, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), whose nature is unimpeded sovereignty, when contracted, becomes the *āṇava-mala*, which consists of the state of feeling incomplete.

The power of knowledge, through gradual contraction, results in the attainment of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) from omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) due to differentiation; this occurs by assuming extreme contraction, preceded by the transformation into the internal organ, the intellect, and the sense organs.
The impurity of māyā consists in the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition.
Through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), as the capacity for universal agency gradually attains the state of limited agency within differentiation,
it first assumes the contraction of the form of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) and subsequently reaches a state of extreme limitation.
The karmic impurity consists of the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions.

Likewise, the powers of universal agency, omniscience, fullness, eternity, and pervasiveness, while undergoing contraction, manifest respectively in the form of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*.
And such a transmigrating being (saṃsārī) is said to be impoverished in power; however, when his own power unfolds,
he is indeed Śiva himself.

[Objection: "But in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), does this [Self] possess any characteristic mark appropriate to Śiva, by virtue of which it is proclaimed that Śiva himself exists in such a state? [The author] says: "Yes, there is; nevertheless, like him, he performs the fivefold cosmic acts. (10)
In this regard, this is precisely the distinction of the non-dualistic vision of Īśvara from the proponents of Brahman:

"We bow to the God who is the agent of creation and dissolution, the cause of preservation and absorption, the bestower of grace, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who take refuge in him. [13]
According to the principle taught in the *Śrīmat-Svacchanda* and other scriptures, the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is eternally engaged in the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*).
And just as the Lord [manifests] through the process of expanding the pure and impure paths...

Just as He performs the acts of creation and so forth, which consist of the unfolding of His own essential nature, so too does He carry out the fivefold functions even within the realm of transmigratory existence by means of His contracted power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). To explain further:
Thus, even in the realm of conventional discourse, the Lord, entering the body and so forth,
may by his own will manifest externally the very mass of objects that is already shining within.

Thus, according to the view of the meaning expressed in the *Pratyabhijñākārikā*, when the Great Lord, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), enters the state of the body, vital breath, and so forth, and at the occasion of becoming extroverted (*bahirmukhībhāva*), manifests an object such as "blue" with its specific spatial and temporal determinations, then His agency (*sraṣṭṛtā*) resides in that aspect of the manifestation of the specific space, time, and so on.

In the aspect of the manifestation of other places, times, and so forth, it possesses the quality of being a destroyer; in the aspect of the manifestation of blue and so forth, it possesses the quality of being a sustainer; and in the aspect of the manifestation of differentiation, it possesses the quality of effecting dissolution.
The state of being a benefactor occurs when [the Lord] manifests through the unity of light;
and how the Blessed One always performs the fivefold activity has been explained by me at length in the *Spandasandoha*.

It is thus established: this fivefold performance of duties, when constantly cultivated with firm practice as one's own, certainly brings forth the sovereignty of Maheśvara for those who possess devotion.
For this very reason, those who constantly cultivate this [realization] are declared to be *jīvanmukta*s, knowing the universe as consisting of the expansion of their own true nature;
whereas those who do not do so are [bound] in every respect.
Perceiving the various objects of measurement as distinct from themselves, they are bound souls.
And this is not the only mode [of action] regarding the performance of the fivefold function; rather, there is also another of a secret nature, as he says:
"by means of manifestation, attraction, contemplation, establishing the seed-state, and dissolution."
Those [are as follows]: // 11 //
The phrase "he performs the fivefold activities" is connected from the preceding context.
Through the venerable vision of the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*), whatever appears by way of the sequential expansion of the goddesses beginning with Dṛk (Vision) is that which is created.
Thus, when that state has been created and one remains impassively attached to it for some time, then it is established by the Goddess of Stability (*sthitidevī*).
However, at the moment of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), which is synonymous with wonder (*camatkāra*), it is withdrawn.
As it was said by Śrī Rāma:
"The mountain of duality, which cannot be split even by the diamond of meditative absorption (samādhivajra) or by others,
has been grasped and destroyed by those endowed with the power of devotion to you."

But when, even while being withdrawn, this [mind] deposits internal latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) such as various doubts and so forth, then it has attained the state of being a seed for the future arising of saṃsāra, and the stage of dissolution is merely superimposed upon it.

Furthermore, when that [object], having been thus established within, or even another object being experienced, undergoes transformation into the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*) through the method of forceful digestion (*haṭhapāka*) by means of the technique of total absorption (*alaṃgrāsa*), then it is indeed graced by the attainment of fullness. And such is...

Although the capacity to perform the fivefold function is always present in everyone, it does not manifest without the instruction of a true guru; therefore, service to the true guru alone must be pursued for the sake of its manifestation.

Furthermore, he states that for one who lacks this thorough knowledge without the instruction of a true guru, there arises a state of delusion caused by one's own powers (*śakti*), which conceal their true nature.
When that is not fully understood, being deluded by one's own powers constitutes the state of transmigratory existence. // 12 //

When this fivefold performance of action, which is constantly occurring, is not fully understood, there is an absence of the unfolding of one's own power caused by the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*); consequently, due to the non-manifestation [of that power], one remains deluded by one's own powers, pinned down by the spikes of various worldly and scriptural doubts— this very state is what [is meant].
This is the state of being in saṃsāra.
As it is said in the venerable *Sarvavīrabhaṭṭāraka*:
"Due to ignorance, the world fears; from that [fear] come creation and dissolution."
"All mantras consist of phonemes, and all phonemes consist of Śiva.

For it is thus: this supreme power of speech (parāvāk-śakti), which is non-different from the light of consciousness, whose nature is the eternally manifest Great Mantra, and which consists of the perfect self-reflection of "I" (pūrṇāhaṃvimarśa).
Containing within her womb the entire wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) whose forms range from *a* to *kṣa*,
she first manifests the stage of the subject through the sequence of *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and so forth;
and therein, by not manifesting her own true nature (*svarūpa*) as the supreme form (*parārūpa*), she [functions] for the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*).
It brings forth at every moment a fresh act of conceptualization, which consists in the appearance of indistinct and non-common objects;
furthermore, it shows even the pure stage of non-conceptuality as being veiled by that [conceptualization].
And therein, deluded by the various powers of the letters beginning with *ka*, which are presided over by deities such as Brāhmī and others,
the foolish person considers the limited, dependent body, vital breath, and so forth, to be the Self.
The goddesses such as Brāhmī and others [exercise] creation and maintenance within the domain of duality during the state of bondage (*paśu*), and within the domain of non-duality...
While manifesting withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), they merely bring about the state of being a vessel for limited conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
But in the state of the Consort (*patnī-daśā*), manifesting withdrawal within difference and emanation and maintenance within non-difference,
they progressively lead to the entry into the venerable Bhairava-mudrā through the gradual reduction of conceptualization.
They open up the very great stage of non-conceptuality for one who fully understands,
"All this is my own manifestation";
even amidst the proliferation of conceptualizations, there is the state of Great Lordship for one whose self is the universe.
In this manner, they cause the power of pure conceptualization (*śuddhavikalpa-śakti*)—which is immersed in the absorption of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*)—to manifest.

Consequently, according to the principle stated, the very state of being deluded by one's own powers constitutes transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). Furthermore, the Blessed Lady, who is the power of consciousness itself, is called *Vāmā* because she emits the universe and because her conduct is contrary to worldly norms.

Known as Vāmeśvarī, she is the virtuous one who, in the form of Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī, manifests through all the natures of subjects, internal organs, external organs, and objective entities; yet,
within the state of the bound soul (paśu), she rests in the plane of the void.

It shines by means of the *khecarīcakra*, which consists of the powers such as *kalā* whose nature is limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*) and so forth, and whose essential form is the concealment of the state of moving within the sky of ultimate consciousness (*pāramārthikacidgaganacarītva*).

It [shines] by means of the *gocarīcakra*, which takes the form of the goddesses of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whose primary functions are the determination of duality, self-conceit, and conceptualization (*vikalpana*).
It manifests as its ultimate essential nature, which consists of the concealment of the non-dual certainty [of identity];
and it flashes forth through the *dikcarī*-circle, whose essence is the deities of the external senses primarily characterized by the perception of duality,
as its ultimate essential nature, which consists of the manifestation of concealed non-duality, from all sides.
And by means of the wheel of the earth-dwellers (*bhūcarīcakra*), which has as its nature objects of knowledge appearing as discrete,

which conceals its own all-pervasive essential form, and which deludes the hearts of bound souls (*paśu*), [the Self] shines forth. But on the level of the Lord (*pati*), it shines as the sky-farer of consciousness (*cidgaganacarī*), whose essence consists of the powers such as universal agency.
She shines forth as the *gocarī* through the nature of the ascertainment of non-duality; as the *dikcarī* through the nature of the intuition of non-duality;

and as the *bhūcarī* through the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) whose essence is the manifestation of non-duality, which is like one's own limb, and which expands the heart of the Lord.
Thus it has been said by him who possesses unartificial reverence born from the wonder of the innate (*sahaja*).

Bhaṭṭa Dāmodara states in his *Vimuktaka* verses: "The deities beginning with Vāmeśā reside within and without the senses, both in their complete and limited forms; through knowledge or ignorance of them, they bestow liberation or bondage."

And thus, the very state of transmigratory existence consists in being deluded by one's own power. Moreover, for the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, there is His own, inseparable, and singular agency, the essence of which is radiant manifestation (*sphurattā*).

The power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-śakti*). When that [power], having concealed its own nature, abides in the state of bondage (*pāśava*) through the conditions of the powers of prāṇa, apāna, and samāna, and through the stages of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
And through the body, vital breath, the city of eight, and the kalās, [the Lord] causes delusion; that state of being deluded by those is transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva).
But when [one realizes] the power of udāna, which shines forth in the central abode and whose essence is the pervasion of the universe—
And when one unfolds the power of *vyāna*, which consists of the state of the fourth (*turya*) and the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), as a mass of consciousness and bliss,

then even while in the condition of the body and so forth, there occurs the state of the Lord, which is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Thus, the threefold delusion caused by one's own power has been explained.

In the sūtra [16], "cidvat," it was stated that the conscious light (citprakāśa) which has assumed contraction is the transmigrating being (saṃsārī). Here, however, it is stated by another method that his state of transmigration arises through being deluded by his own power (svaśakti). Thus, even when one possesses contracted powers and the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, if he is not deluded by his own power...

Then, according to the established tradition of the scriptures (*āmnāya*) that "this embodied one is the Supreme Lord," it is described by way of this formulation that [the teachers] are indeed the venerable Śiva himself:
"Having assumed human bodies, those Supreme Lords remain concealed."

And it is said in the *Pratyabhijñāṭīkā*: "Even those who perceive the body itself, or even a jar and so forth, as consisting of the thirty-six principles and having the nature of Śiva, they too attain perfection."

In order to demonstrate the vision of reality as the antidote to the meaning of the aforementioned sūtras, he says: "Upon the thorough knowledge of that, it is consciousness itself which, through its inward-turning nature, ascends to the state of volition; thus, it is pure awareness (citi). // 13 //
In connection with the explanation of the preceding sūtra, this sūtra has already been explained at length from the perspective of the objects of cognition (*prameya*);
however, it is now explained according to the sequence of the words.
Of that [object] which belongs to oneself...

When there is full comprehension of the performance of the fivefold activity, because the cause characterized by non-comprehension has been removed, and because the delusion regarding one's own power has ceased, one attains sovereignty. Thus, that very mind previously explained—
which was contracting and extroverted— by abandoning its extroversion through becoming introverted, [attains this state].

By ascending the plane of volition (*cetanā*) through the process of traversing the levels of the subject (*grāhaka*), and by the dissolution even of the subtle trace of contraction (*saṃkocakalā*), consciousness becomes its own true nature;
it attains its own supreme state, which consists of pure consciousness.
The meaning is "it enters."

Now, one might object: "If the state of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is ultimately real and its very nature is the swallowing of all duality, then even in the state of *māyā* it must remain of that same nature, just as the sun, even when obscured by clouds, continues to manifest objects. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The fire of consciousness, even when concealed at the stage of ascent by its own substrate, consumes the fuel of the objects of cognition. // 14 //
Citi alone is fire because of its nature of devouring the universe;
even though it is concealed in the state of descent— that is, within the subjectivity of Māyā— and although its essential nature is veiled by its own sovereignty.

Like a fire covered by abundant ash, it consumes—that is, assimilates into its own nature—the fuel of objects of cognition such as blue, yellow, and so forth, by means of a mere measure or portion (*mātrayā*). The intended meaning of the word "measure" (*mātrā*) is this: even while swallowing [the object], it does not do so through its totality (*sārvātmyena*).
Rather, it consumes [the object] partially, yet causes it to arise by means of its nature as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
And the state of being a consumer is established for all subjects through their own direct experience alone. As was stated by the venerable Utpaladeva in his *Nijastotra*:
"All living beings without exception—even Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu—exist as they are swallowed by you; therefore, O God, I bow to the universe which consists of you. [18] Thus [it is said].

When, however, having accomplished the expansion and contraction of the Mistress of the Instruments (karaṇeśvarī), she enters into the method of practicing the sequence of emanation and withdrawal, then, upon attaining power, she assimilates the universe to herself. // 15 //

Citi itself is *bala* (power), which, by immersing its own nature within the concealment of the body, vital breaths, and so forth, expands it through the state of emergence (*unmajjana*). As it has been said:
"Having seized that power, the mantras... [19].

And thus, upon attaining power and resorting to the emergent nature of one's own being, one assimilates the entire universe— from the earth up to Sadāśiva— into oneself, manifesting it as non-different from one's own essential nature.
This has been stated by the former teachers in the *Kramasūtras*, which are composed in their own vernacular:
Just as a fire, once ignited, consumes whatever is to be burned, so too should one devour the snares of sense objects.
It should not be argued that the state of immersion (*samāveśa*), which consists in the assimilation of the universe into the Self, is merely occasional;
for how could this [state] be something to be adopted, given that it occurs through the process of the emergence and submergence of the body and other such factors?
Its occasional nature appears as if it were real;
however, in reality,
its occasional character arises solely from the emergence of the body and other such factors manifested through the sovereignty of consciousness.
This [consciousness], however, is always manifest;
otherwise, even that body and so forth would not be manifest.
For this very reason, there is practice for the purpose of submerging the conceit of being a subject (pramātṛtā) with respect to the body and so forth, but not...
The venerable authors of the *Pratyabhijñā* maintain that this is for the purpose of attaining the state of the subject, which is the essence of eternal and primordial non-prostration.
And thus,

when the bliss of consciousness is attained, the firm realization of identity with consciousness even while the body and other objects are being perceived is *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). // 16 //

When the bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*), which consists of immersion (*samāveśa*) in the nature of the universal self (*viśvātmasātkāra*), has been attained, then even when the body, vital breath, objects such as blue, and pleasure appear during the state of emergence (*vyutthānadaśā*) like mere petals,
that [bliss] persists by the power of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of immersion, reinforced by the sequence of reasoning to be set forth.
The firm realization of the identity with consciousness;

that very unswerving manifestation of oneness with consciousness is *jīvanmukti*— liberation even while living, while still maintaining the vital breaths— because the entire mass of fetters has been dissolved by one who has recognized his own true nature.
As it is said in the Spandaśāstra:
"He whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play, seeing thus and being constantly disciplined, is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (20)

Now, he says that the attainment of the bliss of consciousness occurs somehow through the expansion of the center: "From the expansion of the middle, there is the attainment of the bliss of consciousness. (17)

Because it exists as the most intimate interiority of all, and because the essential nature of anything whatsoever cannot be established without being grounded upon it, the Blessed Consciousness alone is the center.
However, in the state of *māyā*, it...

Even though it is of such a nature, having concealed its own true form, it assumes the state of the power of *prāṇa* according to the principle that "first consciousness is transformed into *prāṇa*"; then, descending in order, it rests upon the planes of the intellect, the body, and so forth, following the course of the thousands of channels (*nāḍīsahasra*).

And even there, according to the analogy of the Palāśa leaf’s central vein, it exists predominantly as the form of the central channel (madhyamanāḍī), which has the power of breath (prāṇaśakti) as its support, extending from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) down to the downward-facing mouth.

Because all mental fluctuations arise from that very source and find their rest in that very place, even though consciousness is of such a nature, it remains with its true form closed off for bound souls (paśus).
However, when—by the sequence of reasoning already stated—it becomes the central consciousness existing as the innermost of all; [21]
If the Blessed One blossoms— or if, according to the sequence to be described, the central *brahmanāḍī* blossoms—
then from that blossoming there occurs the attainment, or acquisition, of the bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*) in the form previously mentioned;
and from that, the aforementioned liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) follows.
He states the reasoning for the expansion of the center:

"In this context, the means [to liberation] consist of the destruction of conceptual construction, the contraction and expansion of power, the cutting of the flow [of breath], and the contemplation of the initial and final limits. (18)
In this context, regarding the expansion of the central power (*madhya-śakti*), the means consist of the cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

It has already been stated that the expansion of consciousness, which is the very center of all things, arises by following the previously taught performance of the fivefold cosmic act (*pañca-kṛtya*) and other such functions.
However, another method is also taught:

by severing all the constraints and bonds of mechanical systems such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and mudrās, one who has fixed the mind in the heart should, according to the stated reasoning, [dissolve] the conceptual construction that obstructs one's own abiding state through this very easy means.

By not thinking of anything at all, pacifying [the mind] through non-conceptual discernment, and being intent upon beholding the stainless, pure consciousness as the subject— untainted by the body and so forth— one very soon attains the state of absorption in the Turyātīta (beyond the fourth), wherein the unfolding expansion is manifest.
"Through the abandonment of conceptual construction and one-pointedness, the state of lordship is attained gradually.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*, and likewise in the *Śrī-Spanda*.
"When agitation is dissolved, then the supreme state arises. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Śrījñānagarbha*:
"O Mother, having abandoned all mental activities in every respect..."

"By Your power, that supreme state— which blazes with freedom from dependence on the performance of actions and their fruits— is suddenly realized by men who remain steadfast, as it pours forth the nectar of tireless and peerless bliss. Thus [it is said].
And this method is stated first because it is the most prominent and because it has already been established in the *Pratyabhijñā*.

Although the contraction of power (*śaktisaṃkoca*) and other such factors were not explained in the *Pratyabhijñā*, they are nevertheless demonstrated by us here as an incidental digression, since they are part of the traditional teaching (*āmnāyika*). For in many cases...
Among those who have been shown [the path], someone will enter by means of something.
The contraction of power (*śakti*) is the process of turning inward, by way of the sense-faculties, through the sequence of withdrawal even as it is flowing outward. As it has been said:
In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the fourth Vallī, in its first verse, it is said:
"The Self-existent pierced the openings outward;
therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self."
"A certain wise man beheld the inner self, with his eyes turned inward, attaining immortality.
Thus it is said; or else, even though [the mind] has gone outward, it is withdrawn like the limbs of a tortoise, or like entering the heart at a time of fear.
It is the withdrawal from everything, as it has been said: "When that [limitation] is removed, there is a state of eternal manifestation.
It is the expansion of power (*śakti*), which, though hidden within, occurs simultaneously through the unfolding of the entire wheel of the senses.
"With the internal as the object and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking and opening," thus [it is said].
By means of the method of entering the mudrā of Bhairava, there is an outward expansion. As it has been stated:
"All powers, such as seeing and so forth, [are perceived] by the mind."
"Having simultaneously cast [all things] everywhere upon their respective objects of knowledge, you remain in the center like a pillar of gold;
as the one support of the universe, you shine forth. Thus.
The venerable Bhaṭṭakallaṭa has also stated: "Its establishment [is] through the transformation within form and the other [sensory objects].

Furthermore, the contraction and expansion of power occurs by means of the subtle vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) arising through the sequence of the pulsation of the nostrils, resulting in the piercing of the *bhru* [center].

One should cultivate the state of the expansion and its resting in the station of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī attained through gradual stages; and having rectified the power within the downward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, who is the form of the sixth face,
one should achieve immersion by touching the ground of her root, her tip, and her middle.
As it is said in the *Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
"One should cast the mind, consisting of bliss, into the midst of fire and poison;
or, being filled solely with wind, one is joined with the bliss of passion. [26]
Here, fire is the ground of contraction through the process of entry;
it is the locus of poison by way of expansion, according to the meaning of the root *viṣḷ* as "to pervade."

The "cutting" (*cheda*) of the two currents, namely the *prāṇa* and *apāna* moving to the left and right, is their severance preceded by resting in the heart through the internal utterance of mostly vowel-less syllables such as *ka* and *ha*.

As it is said in the *Jñānagarbha*: "For one whose mind is held within the interior of the heart-lotus, which severs the two side-channels that have extended far and wide, having been made motionless by the breathless [state]..."
"This sprout of knowledge, which has split open the blinding darkness, rises within you; it is capable of producing supreme lordship even in a bound soul.
Thus, the "original limit" (ādikoṭi) is the Heart.

The "end-limit" (antakoṭi) is the "twelve-finger space" (dvādaśānta). The "contemplation" (nibhālana) of these two at the moment of the arousal and repose of the vital breath (prāṇa) is the cultivation [of that state] by means of fixing the mind.
As it is said in the Vijñānabhairava:
"With the senses dissolved in the space of the heart, situated within the hollow of the lotus, with a mind focused on nothing else, O fortunate one, one shall attain supreme fortune.
Thus it is said; in whatever manner and wherever it may be, one should cast the mind into the *dvādaśānta*.

"Day by day, there will be a distinct difference for one whose activity has diminished at every moment. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the cultivation of the state of *unmeṣa* is intended. As it has been said:
"That indeed should be known as *unmeṣa*; one should perceive it for oneself."
Thus it is stated in the *Spanda*:
likewise, the savoring of delightful objects and so forth are also included,
as has been said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava* itself.

Through the unfolding of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (rasa) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; thus, one becomes composed of great bliss (mahānanda).

For the yogin whose self is unified with the incomparable bliss of savoring objects such as song and the like, there arises the state of being that very object through its ascent into the mind by way of identification with it.

"Wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, one should fix the mind right there; in each such place, the nature of supreme bliss is fully revealed. Thus, other practices as well—such as the meditation on one's own self as full of bliss—should be understood accordingly. So it is said.
These and others are the means for the expansion of the middle here.
From the expansion of the center, there is the attainment of consciousness-bliss;
and that alone is the samādhi of the supreme yogi, synonymous with terms such as "total immersion" (samāveśa) and "attainment of equality" (samapatti).
He states the reasoning for its state of being eternally arisen:

"In the state of emergence (vyutthāna) characterized by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of meditative absorption (samādhi), through the repeated awareness of identity with consciousness (cidaikya), there is the attainment of eternally arisen absorption. (19)

The excellent yogin, having attained immersion, even during the state of emergence, is as if intoxicated by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the flavor of samādhi; reeling with bliss, he perceives the multitude of objective phenomena dissolving like fragments of autumn clouds into the very sky of consciousness,
and repeatedly takes recourse in that inward-turned state alone.

By means of the process of the meditative absorption of closing [the eyes], while contemplating the very oneness of consciousness, one becomes of a single flavor with that absorption even at the time intended for emergence from it;
as it is said in the *Kramasūtras*:

“By means of the sequential mudrā, which has its internal nature, the practitioner becomes externally oriented and enters [the state]. In that regard, first there is entry from the external into the internal, and then entry from the internal into the external nature.”
"By the power of immersion (āveśa), this sequence of mudrās arises, both external and internal.

Herein the meaning is as follows: by means of that fourth power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), which is the *kramamudrā*, one "seals" (*mudrayati*)—that is, renders well-established and assimilates to oneself—the sequence whose nature consists of the wheels of consciousness (*saṃviccakra*) pertaining to emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.

"Internally" means by way of the nature of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness). "Externally directed," even while engaged with sense objects, the practitioner who is fully absorbed and has directly realized the expansion of the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) becomes a supreme yogin.
And therein, from the external collection of objects being swallowed up, [he moves] internally into the supreme ground of consciousness.

Entry, which is immersion, occurs precisely through the process of devouring; and it arises solely by virtue of immersion— that is, by the power of immersion— resulting from the direct realization of the internal nature of the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*).

Through the method of vomiting [the ego], entry occurs into the external nature— the collection of objects appearing as "this-ness"— and thus arises an immersion (*samāveśa*) consisting in the manifestation of the solidification of the essence of consciousness;
this is the "internal-and-external" immersion, which is the self of the eternally arisen immersion, because it bestows *muda*, that is, joy.

Because its nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it dissolves the bonds (*pāśa*), and because it seals the universe within the internal state of the fourth (*turya*), the sequence of the *mudrās* is also called "sequence" (*krama*), since it manifests the sequence of emanation and so forth, and consists of the manifestation of that sequence.
Now he states the fruit of this attainment of samādhi:

"Then, through immersion into the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), which consists of the potency of the Great Mantra whose essence is light and bliss, there is the attainment of lordship over the wheel of one's own consciousness-deities, which constantly effects the emanation and withdrawal of all things."
Thus it is auspicious. // 20 //

When the eternally arisen *samādhi* has been attained, there occurs an immersion (*āveśa*) into that which is the essence of light and bliss, a single mass of the delight of consciousness (*cidāhlāda*),
the great power of the mantra (*mantravīrya*), the life-force of all mantras, the full form of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*),
this very "I-ness" (*ahantā*) which is the uncreated wonder of one's own self; [from this immersion], [the cycle begins] from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) onwards.

The attainment— that is, the reaching— of that sovereignty which consists of one's own wheel of the deities of consciousness (*saṃviddevatācakra*) that effects the diverse creation and dissolution of the universe up to its final limit,
is what is meant; the sense is that this belongs to the supreme yogin who is the subject of the present context.
Thus, the connection [of the passage] is that this entire [universe] is nothing but the very nature of Śiva; this is the conclusion.
In that regard, whatever is perceived as "this" or "something," its very nature is consciousness (*saṃvedana*).
Furthermore, the perceivers (*pramātṛ*), who consist of inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are the reality (*tattva*) of that [consciousness]. Of those [perceivers], too—

For those whose conceit regarding the limitation of adjuncts such as the body has dissolved, the very essence is the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, who possess all bodies. Even of this state, the ultimate reality is the glorious Maheśvara alone, who consists of the wonder of the entire universe brought about by the singular existence of pure Light.
For without the penetration of ultimate luminosity, the manifestation of anything whatsoever is not possible;
and that Supreme Lord, because his essence is absolute freedom (svātantrya), [is that luminosity].
Because it consists of the reflective awareness of the entire mass of sounds from *a* to *kṣa*, which include all illusory phenomena,

it brings about the true state of bliss for the entire universe— comprising both the denoted and the denotative— which has been embraced by it; thus, due to its supreme fullness and freedom from all desire, it is overflowing with the expansion of bliss.
Therefore, starting from the letter *a*, which is the very nature of the Unsurpassed Kula (*anuttarākula*), up to the power-syllable *ha*— which is the expansion of energy (*śaktisphāra*)—

the entire universe that has emerged is internally assimilated by means of the method of contraction (*pratyāhāra*) through the technique of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*) by the letters *a* and *ha* alone, because the letter *kṣa* consists in the cessation of that expansion.
Manifesting as the form of the *bindu*, whose nature is undivided consciousness, it rests in the Absolute (*anuttara*) alone;
thus, this uncreated reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the very essence of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).
For the repose of Light within itself is celebrated as the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*).
And that very rest has been described as arising from the cessation of all dependence.
"Furthermore, autonomy, agency, and even sovereignty are primary.

And this very *ahantā* (I-ness) is the ground of great potency (*vīryabhūmi*), because it is the locus of the arising and resting of all mantras, and because by its power alone they perform their respective purposeful actions. Thus it has been said:
"Having seized that power, the mantras... and so forth,
up to "...these are the followers of the Śiva-dharma," as found in the *Śrīspanda*.
Also in the Śivasūtras:
"From the contemplation of the great lake, there is the experience of the potency of mantra" (36).
Thus, herein, there is immersion into the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), which consists of the potency of the Great Mantra.

By means of the support of attaining that state through the immersion of the body, vital breath, and so forth, there occurs the transformation of the body, the vital breath, and even objects such as "blue" into that [state], by flooding them with its essence.
For indeed, whatever there may be— be it the body, pleasure, or the blue object— [is thus transformed].

Whether it is manifested, determined, remembered, or conceptualized— in every such case, the divine manifestation consisting of the power of consciousness (citiśakti) shines forth as the very foundation.
For without its shining forth, nothing at all could exist.

Because it has been stated that [the Absolute] is "without vibration" (asphuraṇāt), although it alone shines forth in that manner, by virtue of the conceit bestowed through the coloring of the body, blue objects, and so forth, which are manifested by that power of Māyā, it appears as if possessing various distinct natures;
thus it is conceived by the subjects of Māyā in the form of cognition, volition, determination, and so on.
In reality, however, this power of consciousness is one alone. As it has been said:

"That which is this intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), colored by the succession of various objects, is the cognizer whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness; he is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). [37] Thus.

"By the power of *māyā*, that very [power] of the Lord, when its sphere consists of differentiated objects of cognition, is designated by such names as knowledge (*jñāna*), volition (*saṃkalpa*), and determination (*adhyavasāya*). Thus,
if this single power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) alone is manifesting itself in all states, [then...]

Through the method of entering into and supporting that [state], it is attained; because of that immersion and by virtue of the previously mentioned reasoning regarding the sequential opening and closing of the instruments (*karaṇa*), everything consists of everything.
Thus, even during the dissolution of this or that [object], there is that which always effects the creation and dissolution of all things.
The wheel of deities of innate consciousness is a mass of rays from the internal and external senses free from illusion;
therein lies the sovereign empire of lordship, the state of being the Supreme Bhairava, which constitutes the attainment of that [state] for the supreme yogin. As it has been said:
"But when [the mind] is firmly established in one place, then by controlling its dissolution and emergence, it attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, it becomes the Lord of the Wheel.
Here, "in one place" refers to "one should project everything in one place," which is the ground of the vibration of universal consciousness (*citsāmānyaspandabhūḥ*).
The nature of the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*) is to be explained.
By the word "of that" (*tasya*), what was introduced in the passage "confined by the *puryaṣṭaka*" [verse 41] is referred to.

It is the *puryaṣṭaka* alone that must be grasped as the object of contact, and not as the author of the *Vivaraṇa* has explained it— namely, as being either in one place, or in the subtle body, or in the gross body;
and this has been praised by me.
"Independent sovereign of the wheels of consciousness, the Great Lord,
served by the wheel of the deities of awareness— may that certain one be victorious! The word "iti" (thus) marks the conclusion.
All this— the entire body of the topics thus explained—
is indeed Śiva, because it is the cause for attaining Śiva, because it has issued forth from Śiva, and because it is non-different from the very nature of Śiva; may there be auspiciousness!
People, being obstructed at every moment by the body, vital breath, pleasure, and so forth,
do not recognize this consciousness of their own, which belongs to Maheśvara and is a mass of full bliss;
for within the ocean of the nectar of awakening, the entire universe appears on all sides like a mere lump of foam.
He who perceives [the deity] through the oral instruction as it has been described is that one Śiva himself in person.
Those in whom the descent of grace from Śaṅkara has occurred,
yet who— due to a lack of practice— are unfit for sharp logical methods,
are nevertheless capable of knowing the Recognition of the Lord (Īśvarapratyabhijñā).
This instruction on reality has been declared to you concerning them.
This *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya* is completed;
it is the work of the venerable teacher Rājānaka Kṣemarāja, who lives upon the lotus feet of the illustrious Abhinavagupta, the most excellent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
